Don't take anything too seriously, we are trying out best here! - [**Interactive:** Whenever possible, I favor dynamic content over static content]{.hover-emphasize} - **Real-World Examples:** We will use a mixture of real and fabricated data to help illustrate ideas ## What Have You Disliked About Past Stats Courses? 👎 ::: highlight-last - Turn to a neighbor (or shout it out) — what made a past math/stats class miserable? - I can't fix what I don't know about. ::: ## What Are Students Saying? ### My Course Evaluations :::: marquee-wrap ::: marquee-track "Best professor I've ever had" \| "Made 9am class feel like a mid-day class, not boring" \| "Awesome professor, did a great job teaching this class" \|"Favorite professor I have had so far" \| "Super approachable, understanding, and cares about his students" \| "Great instructor — hate statistics" ::: :::: ## Outside of Class ### Hobbies and Media ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Statistics ### About the Course **Statistics** is the science of collecting, analyzing, and interpreting data to make informed decisions. ::: highlight-last - As a **practitioner**, your practices need to be informed by evidence-based treatments - As a **researcher**, your claims need to be supported by evidence that can assert a high probability of a relationship or cause and effect - Because data is everywhere, even in your **Netflix** recommendations! ::: ```{dot} //| fig-align: center digraph { graph [rankdir=LR, bgcolor="transparent"] node [shape="box", style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#DCE8E1", color="#5C715E", fontname="Fira Sans", fontcolor="#2F3E46"] edge [color="#5C715E", penwidth=1.5] Stats[label="Statistics", fillcolor="#8FAF9E", fontcolor="white", style="rounded,filled"] Prac[label="Practitioner\n(evidence-based treatment)"] Res[label="Researcher\n(cause & effect claims)"] Every[label="Everyday Life\n(Netflix, reviews, news)"] Stats -> Prac Stats -> Res Stats -> Every } ``` ## What is Statistics? ### Definition and Terminology Statistics : The field of **describing**, **analyzing**, and making **inferences** based on **data** either from a **sample** or a **population** Describing : What does the data 'look' like? Analyzing : A mathematical approach to extracting information about the data Inferences : Applying logical reasoning to predict what might happen in subsequent measurements. Typically, inferences are made from samples and extrapolated into what the population might be 'expected' to look like. Data : Qualitative or Quantitative information that consists of measured or manipulated variables Sample : A subset of the population of interest Population : The entire set of interest. ## Why is it Important? ### When Do I Use It? Everywhere! Statistics makes appearances anywhere you see information being summarized or being used to make decisions. - [directions_car]{.material-icons .inline-icon} Purchasing a car - You look at reviews and infer the overall takeaway of how 'good' or 'bad' a car might be. - [restaurant]{.material-icons .inline-icon} Going to a restaurant - You base your selection on prior experiences or on reviews/opinions from people you trust - [how_to_vote]{.material-icons .inline-icon} Voting for a candidate - You look for increases in wages and decreases in taxes - You look for promises of pollution reduction and energy increases - [local_movies]{.material-icons .inline-icon} Going to the Movies - You pick a movie based on genre, past experiences, and reviews ## Data Literacy ### Why Do I Need It Statistical and data literacy is useful for being able to make informed decisions — especially when a claim is designed to grab your attention before you've had a chance to think it through. - If you saw a headline claiming that blueberries could cure cancer, wouldn't it be helpful to know how to evaluate that claim before sharing it? 1. How many blueberries, and how "cancer" was even measured? 2. How long do you have to eat them for? 3. Is it all types of cancer or a specific one? 4. Is it truly that blueberries cure cancer, or are they mixed in with something else (diet, exercise, a specific compound at a dose no one eats naturally)? ::: fragment This is the same skill you'll use on every "coffee causes/cures \_\_\_" headline for the rest of your life. ::: ## Too Good to Be True ### Wouldn't it be nice if... We tend to describe the world the way we *wish* it were, not always the way it actually is. A few examples of that: - Dogs smiled *(that "smile" is often a stress signal, not happiness)* - Birdsong is always beautiful *(some of it is territorial alarm-calling)* - All animals love their children *(infanticide is documented across many species)* Our brain is a pattern matching machine - We look for information that confirms our thoughts and surroundings - We would (often) prefer that things were nice and pretty, but reality is often not so simple # What is your future career goal? ## Statistics in Psychology ### How Each Profession Uses Data - Mental Health Counselors/Social Workers - Knowing that a certain percentage of college students suffer from Anxiety, you can improve your outreach and provide material aimed to address and reduce the impact - Human Resources/Training and Development - If 30% of employees report that there are so few incentives and little to no sense of belonging, you can take actionable steps to address those issues - Researchers (Hey That's What I do!) - Hypotheses are only supported when the data suggests that the findings are unlikely to have occurred by chance. - Academia (Hey That's What I do!) - If the Average Exam score is an 85 with a Standard Deviation of 20 points, I have reason to believe that the test was either too difficult or the material was not explained well enough # Raise your hand if you dislike math ## Goals for this Class: 1. Be comfortable looking at data and making inferences 2. Be comfortable looking at graphs and making inferences and gathering takeaways 3. Reading scientific and popular articles and critically thinking about the claims being made 4. Understand what constitutes evidence and what it means for hypotheses to be supported 5. Understand that research is probabilistic # Why Do I Even Need This Course, I'm Going to Be A... ## Why Should You Care? ::: highlight-last - Therapist: - Your practices need to be informed by evidence-based treatments - Researcher: - Your claims need to be supported by evidence that can assert a high probability or relationship or cause and effect. - Non-Data Field: - Because data is everywhere, even in your **Netflix** recommendations! ::: ::: {.flowpic .fragment} ![Flowchart Visual of Netflix Recommendation System](https://mermaid.ink/img/pako:eNpVkl9vgjAUxb9Kc5PtiTlQBORhicL-JkvMdFuy4kMDV2gG7VLKnBq_-wrMTPvU5v7Ovacndw-pzBBCWJdykxZMabKME0HMmdLXGhV5ZzotuMhJJIVGoVfk6uqGzGgkyxJTTd44btpyzDRb9cpZh0R0Kli53SGZK1yjQpFi_UdEHRHTF0xlVaHImOZSkFuRc4F_TNwxt_8MZuRZfnOsrxeF3LStevDigswUE71LLtZl04069XJHjzYfeK2l2p45vaf3KBTW5JIsWV6f1R7ogle8ZIq0afwP7d090qX5V3Yaz2n5ic6NRpoY-M64n_P0s16BBbniGYRaNWhBhapi7RP2rTQBXWCFCYTmmjH1mUAiDkbzxcSHlNVRpmSTF8dH82UCxJizXDFDrFlZt0ibmYpkIzSEIzfoekC4hx8IvYETjDw38B3bdyb20PMs2ELou4PAH3veeDgOfN91RwcLdt1UezBx_KE7tMe249vBJBhZgBk3WT73C9Tt0eEXhcW32g?type=png) ::: ## What You'll Learn This Semester ### Introduction to Research ::: highlight-last - Descriptive Statistics - What does the data 'look like'? - Probability is Paramount - What are the chances this happens and what is the probability this only happens because of chance? - Testing hypotheses - If \[condition\] has this specific attribute, we expect \[event\] to take place. - Correlation, regression, and causation - How are variables related to each other? - How much can variables predict each other? - Does this variable cause a change in this other component? ::: ## Syllabus ### How This Class Works ::: {.badge-row} ::: {.content-badge} [forum]{.material-icons} #### Participation Asking questions helps you understand -- and will likely help your classmates too! ::: ::: {.content-badge} [edit_note]{.material-icons} #### Homework Practice outside of the classroom, kept low-stakes. ::: ::: {.content-badge} [science]{.material-icons} #### Labs A weekly hands-on session right after lecture, applying that week's concepts in R. ::: ::: {.content-badge} [fact_check]{.material-icons} #### Exams A decent (not perfect) way to see how well you understand and can apply the material. ::: ::: Full syllabus, grading breakdown, and office hours are posted on Brightspace — take a few minutes to skim it before next class. # Research Design ### Lecture 1 ## What is Research? Research is a **systematic process** of asking a question about the world and collecting evidence to answer it — as opposed to relying on intuition, anecdote, or "everybody knows that..." ::: highlight-last - It's **systematic**: it follows a planned, repeatable process (not a one-off guess). - It's **testable**: it produces a claim that data could, in principle, prove wrong. - It's **shareable**: the methods and data are reported clearly enough that someone else could check your work. ::: ## What is Research? ### The Basic Cycle ```{dot} //| fig-align: center digraph { graph [bgcolor="transparent"] node [shape="box", style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#DCE8E1", color="#5C715E", fontname="Fira Sans", fontcolor="#2F3E46"] edge [color="#5C715E", penwidth=1.5] A[label="1. Observe\nsomething interesting"] B[label="2. Ask a specific,\nanswerable question"] C[label="3. Form a\nhypothesis"] D[label="4. Collect\ndata"] E[label="5. Analyze the data\n(this is where statistics comes in!)"] F[label="6. Draw a\nconclusion"] A -> B -> C -> D -> E -> F F -> A [label="often leads to\nthe next question", style=dashed, fontsize=11] } ``` ## What Kinds of Research are there? ### Descriptive Research - Goal: **describe** what's happening, without testing cause and effect - Examples: case studies, naturalistic observation, surveys - Tells you *what* is going on, but not *why* ::: {.icon-row} ::: {.icon-row-item} [description]{.material-icons} Case Studies ::: ::: {.icon-row-item} [visibility]{.material-icons} Observation ::: ::: {.icon-row-item} [poll]{.material-icons} Surveys ::: ::: ## What Kinds of Research is there? ### Correlational Research - Goal: measure whether two variables are **related** to one another - You observe variables as they naturally occur — nothing is manipulated - Lets you predict one variable from another, but **cannot** establish that one causes the other ::: {.icon-row} ::: {.icon-row-item} [scatter_plot]{.material-icons} Relationship ::: ::: {.icon-row-item} [compare_arrows]{.material-icons} Two Variables ::: ::: {.icon-row-item} [block]{.material-icons} Not Causation ::: ::: ## What Kinds of Research is there? ### Experimental Research - Goal: test whether one variable **causes** a change in another - The researcher **manipulates** an independent variable (IV) and measures a dependent variable (DV) - Participants are (ideally) **randomly assigned** to conditions, and other variables are controlled - This is the *only* design type that can support a causal claim ::: {.icon-row} ::: {.icon-row-item} [tune]{.material-icons} Manipulate IV ::: ::: {.icon-row-item} [shuffle]{.material-icons} Random Assignment ::: ::: {.icon-row-item} [verified]{.material-icons} Causal Claim ::: ::: ## What Kinds of Research Are there? ### Putting the Vocabulary Together - **Independent Variable (IV):** what the researcher manipulates (or the grouping variable) - **Dependent Variable (DV):** what the researcher measures — the outcome - **Participants, Materials, Procedure, Design:** the four building blocks you'll use to describe *how* a study was run - You'll get hands-on practice with this vocabulary in **Lab 1**, when we write a Method section together. ## Any Questions? ### I Am an Open Book! ::: book-anim 📕📖 :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
